items.card: Address the Ghost in the Machine
items.lead: Learn what a system is optimising for.
items.body: Recommendation engines, chatbots and automated decision-makers all have incentives of their own.

items.card: Address the Ghost in the Machine
items.lead: Watch for behaviour nobody programmed.
items.body: Even a system’s own creators can be surprised by it — question what you didn’t expect, and where it came from.

items.card: Address the Ghost in the Machine
items.lead: Demand to know how a decision was reached.
items.body: Not just what it was, and back the platforms that make their reasoning visible.

items.card: Address the Ghost in the Machine
items.lead: Find where you can actually intervene.
items.body: If that control point doesn’t exist, push for it to be built in.

items.card: Address the Ghost in the Machine
items.lead: Practise algorithmic hygiene.
items.body: Adjust your settings and feedback regularly, so bias doesn’t quietly harden into the system’s habits.

items.card: Address the Ghost in the Machine
items.lead: Engage in the public debate on how these systems are governed.
items.body: Back policies that build in real ethical guidelines and accountability, not just ones that look good on paper.

items.card: Address the Ghost in the Machine
items.lead: Choose tools that make you sharper, not just faster.
items.body: Look for what augments your own judgement and creativity, not what simply automates the task.

items.card: Address the Ghost in the Machine
items.lead: Build your AI-complementary skills.
items.body: Critical thinking, emotional intelligence, creativity and ethical reasoning are what a machine can’t do for you.

items.card: Address the Ghost in the Machine
items.lead: Insist on human-in-the-loop review for real decisions.
items.body: Especially where the stakes are high, someone should have to approve it, not just see it.

items.card: Address the Ghost in the Machine
items.lead: Build auditable AI from day one.
items.body: Log and monitor every decision, input and algorithmic pathway, not just the ones that go wrong.

items.card: Address the Ghost in the Machine
items.lead: Choose models a person can actually understand.
items.body: Favour interpretable approaches over black boxes wherever you genuinely can.

items.card: Address the Ghost in the Machine
items.lead: Name who is accountable before something breaks.
items.body: Designer, deployer or operator — decide which, in advance, not after.

items.card: Address the Ghost in the Machine
items.lead: Test for bias, misuse and adversarial attack, not just function.
items.body: Do it in diverse real-world conditions, not only the controlled ones.

items.card: Address the Ghost in the Machine
items.lead: Build in a real kill switch.
items.body: Human override and emergency shutdown should be explicit and easy to reach, not theoretical.

items.card: Address the Ghost in the Machine
items.lead: Write regulation that can keep pace with the technology.
items.body: Balance innovation against genuine safeguards and public safety — not one at the expense of the other.

items.card: Address the Ghost in the Machine
items.lead: Put technologists, ethicists, social scientists and policymakers in the same room.
items.body: The consequences of what gets built reach well past the codebase.

items.card: Address the Ghost in the Machine
items.lead: Keep training developers and users on the ethics, not just the features.
items.body: The implications don’t end at launch, and neither should the education.

items.card: Address the Ghost in the Machine
items.lead: Apply the precautionary principle to high-impact systems.
items.body: Prioritise real safety measures and genuine public consensus before wide deployment, not after.

items.lead: Use a password manager.
items.body: Stop recycling passwords — a breach on one site can compromise every account that shares it. A password manager generates unique, high-entropy passwords for everything and leaves you only one master password to remember.

items.lead: Enable Two-Factor Authentication.
items.body: A second verification step — ideally a TOTP app like Google or Microsoft Authenticator rather than SMS, which is vulnerable to SIM-swapping — breaks the attack even if your password is stolen. Prioritise it on email, banking, cloud storage and social media.

items.lead: Practise digital hygiene.
items.body: Enable automatic updates on every device — computers, phones, routers, smart home systems. The gap between a patch's release and its installation is the window criminals actively scan for.

items.lead: Spot the phish.
items.body: Be sceptical of messages built on urgency or unrealistic reward, verify the sender's actual domain, and navigate to official sites directly rather than clicking embedded links.

items.lead: Beware impersonation and pretexting.
items.body: Criminals posing as banks, IT desks or officials will never legitimately ask for your password or 2FA code by email or text — call back on a company's published number if in doubt.

items.lead: Adopt a zero-trust mindset.
items.body: Treat every unexpected message, attachment or link as unproven until you've verified it yourself, even when the sender looks familiar.

items.lead: Limit what you share.
items.body: Criminals target the 'Big Three' — your mother's maiden name, first pet, and childhood address — the trivial details behind most security questions.

items.lead: Control your privacy settings.
items.body: Public profiles make an attacker's reconnaissance effortless, mapping your schedule and vacation status for a perfectly timed spear-phishing message.

items.lead: Question quizzes and surveys.
items.body: Playful prompts like 'what's your superhero name?' are often data-harvesting tools built to mimic common security-question formats.

items.lead: Implement the 3-2-1 backup rule.
items.body: Keep three copies of your data on two different media, with one copy stored offsite — the strongest defence against ransomware.

items.lead: Review your statements regularly.
items.body: Fraud often starts with small test charges of only a few pounds before it escalates — catch them early.

items.lead: Act immediately if compromised.
items.body: Isolate the device from the network, change every password from a clean device, enable 2FA everywhere, and report the incident — time is what matters most.

items.lead: Security isn't an app, a subscription, or a compliance checkbox.
items.body: It's a habit — every password changed, every update applied, every message questioned makes you harder to exploit. Your defence begins the moment you decide not to be an easy target.

items.lead: Schedule digital downtime.
items.body: Designate specific times each day or week to be completely offline — especially during meals, family time, and before bed.

items.lead: Disable unnecessary notifications.
items.body: Turn off all non-essential alerts to reduce interruptions and reclaim your attention.

items.lead: Curate your feeds.
items.body: Actively unfollow, mute or block accounts and content that harm your mood, foster comparison, or distract from your goals.

items.lead: Use technology to support you, not distract you.
items.body: Leverage apps for mindfulness, focus or productivity — but be discerning about which genuinely add value without creating new dependencies.

items.lead: Practise conscious consumption.
items.body: Approach social media with a critical eye, recognising that content is often curated and not a full reflection of reality.

items.lead: Prioritise connection over comparison.
items.body: Use platforms to genuinely connect with friends and family, rather than passively consuming content that sparks envy.

items.lead: Limit doomscrolling.
items.body: Notice the pull to endlessly scroll through negative news or content, and set real limits on how long you engage with it.

items.lead: Practise digital empathy.
items.body: Stay mindful of how your own posts affect others, and help foster a culture of positivity and support.

items.lead: Invest in offline hobbies.
items.body: Engage in activities that don't involve screens — reading physical books, spending time in nature, exercising, or pursuing creative arts.

items.lead: Nurture in-person relationships.
items.body: Dedicate quality time to face-to-face interactions with friends and family, practising active listening and genuine engagement.

items.lead: Create tech-free zones.
items.body: Designate specific areas in your home — the dining table, the bedroom — as phone-free or screen-free zones.

items.lead: Practise mindfulness.
items.body: Cultivate techniques like meditation or mindful breathing to be present in the moment and observe your thoughts without judgement.

items.lead: Demand human-centred design.
items.body: Support companies and initiatives that prioritise user well-being over raw engagement metrics.

items.lead: Push for transparency.
items.body: Advocate for clear disclosure on how algorithms work and how data is used to influence user behaviour.

items.lead: Support regulation.
items.body: Encourage policies that protect digital well-being — covering privacy, data exploitation, and manipulative design patterns.

items.lead: Pay attention to what content appears in your feed, and ask why.
items.body: Notice whether it genuinely interests you, or whether it's designed to provoke a reaction.

items.lead: Drastically reduce your social media notifications.
items.body: Regaining control over when and how you engage starts with cutting the interruptions built to pull you back in.

items.lead: Use built-in app timers or external tools to cap your usage.
items.body: A visible limit turns an open-ended habit into something you can actually choose to stop.

items.lead: Unfollow accounts that don't add value or leave you feeling worse.
items.body: Prioritise genuine connections over a large follower count.

items.lead: Consider your intention before you share anything.
items.body: Are you seeking validation, sharing genuinely, or simply reacting?

items.lead: Studies conformity, social comparison and validation-seeking online.
items.body: Explains why group dynamics in online environments can pull behaviour in a particular direction.

items.lead: Researches user experience design across social platforms.
items.body: Covers the impact of infinite scroll, notifications and feedback mechanisms on behaviour.

items.lead: Studies the psychological and sociological impacts of social media use.
items.body: Includes effects on mental health, self-esteem and political polarisation.

items.lead: Analyses how social networks grow and spread information.
items.body: Shows how the connections between people shape what spreads, and what influence follows.

items.lead: Examines how platforms shape cultural practices and identity.
items.body: Looks at how community and identity form inside digital spaces.

items.lead: The aim of this pause isn't to boycott technology — it's to become a critical user of it.
items.body: Recognising when your behaviour is being influenced lets you make conscious choices, and use technology on your own terms rather than being used by it.

items.card: Navigate the Ethics of Algorithmic Intelligence
items.lead: Understand how the system decides.
items.body: Learn what training data feeds the model, the difference between correlation and causation, and question every personalised recommendation you're shown — a job screening, a loan outcome, a news feed.

items.card: Navigate the Ethics of Algorithmic Intelligence
items.lead: Know when you're facing a black box.
items.body: Many AI models can't explain their own reasoning. That opacity is exactly what makes catching and correcting bias difficult.

items.card: Navigate the Ethics of Algorithmic Intelligence
items.lead: Insist on disclosure and an explanation.
items.body: Support requirements for companies and governments to state plainly when AI is deciding and explain that reasoning in terms you understand — and ask directly when an outcome affects you, why an application was rejected, why a price changed.

items.card: Navigate the Ethics of Algorithmic Intelligence
items.lead: Back open models over sealed ones.
items.body: Open-source AI can be scrutinised by a wider community for bias and ethical concern. Encourage its development and use.

items.card: Navigate the Ethics of Algorithmic Intelligence
items.lead: Remember the data carries the history.
items.body: AI systems learn from historical data that already reflects human bias, stereotype and inequality. Support more representative training data and test outcomes across demographic groups before deployment, not after someone has already been harmed.

items.card: Navigate the Ethics of Algorithmic Intelligence
items.lead: Keep a human able to override the machine.
items.body: Insist on oversight and intervention mechanisms, particularly for high-stakes decisions, so a biased output can be corrected, not just recorded.

items.card: Navigate the Ethics of Algorithmic Intelligence
items.lead: Name who answers when it goes wrong.
items.body: Developer, deployer, user, or the algorithm itself — accountability has to sit somewhere specific, not dissolve into 'the system decided.' Push for legal and regulatory frameworks that address AI liability and give people harmed an actual route to redress.

items.card: Navigate the Ethics of Algorithmic Intelligence
items.lead: Build ethical review into the organisation.
items.body: Internal boards or teams responsible for the ethical development and deployment of AI keep the question live before launch, not just after complaint.

items.card: Navigate the Ethics of Algorithmic Intelligence
items.lead: Take part in the argument, not just the outcome.
items.body: The public conversation about AI's ethical implications shapes what gets built next. Support organisations and policy work building ethical guidelines and regulation at local, national and international level.

items.card: Navigate the Ethics of Algorithmic Intelligence
items.lead: Put human wellbeing ahead of efficiency.
items.body: Insist that fairness, privacy and autonomy are designed in from the start — not treated as costs to trade off against profit.

items.card: Navigate the Ethics of Algorithmic Intelligence
items.lead: Ethics is not a checkbox at the end of the build.
items.body: It's the discipline that decides whether the system deserves the trust it's asking for — practised in the design room, not bolted on after deployment.

items.lead: Block out time for silence or unstructured thought each day.
items.body: Even ten to fifteen minutes is enough to notice the difference.

items.lead: Establish tech-free zones in your home.
items.body: The dining table or the bedroom — anywhere background digital noise doesn't get to follow you.

items.lead: Leave your headphones off during commutes sometimes.
items.body: Let your mind wander or simply observe what's around you, instead of filling the gap.

items.lead: Resist the urge to immediately fill moments of boredom.
items.body: See what thoughts or ideas surface once your mind is actually given the space.

items.lead: Question what you play in the background.
items.body: Ask whether it's genuinely enhancing what you're doing, or just filling a void.

items.lead: Studies the effects of concurrent task performance.
items.body: Including the switching costs that come from moving between tasks.

items.lead: Researches how digital and auditory environments shape behaviour.
items.body: Covers the effects on mood and cognitive performance too.

items.lead: Explores the brain states behind unstructured thought and reflection.
items.body: And how constant external stimulation disrupts them.

items.lead: Examines the benefits of reducing digital input.
items.body: Along with strategies for building a healthier relationship with technology.

items.lead: Looks at how societal change has altered rest and reflection.
items.body: Technology included, in shaping today's patterns of unstructured time.

items.lead: Become the intentional architect of your digital environment.
items.body: Move from being distracted to actively creating your focus — not eliminating technology, but building a personal ecosystem of attention that serves you, not the other way around.

items.lead: Learn how the profiling actually works.
items.body: Understand how your data is collected, how algorithms generally operate, and recognise that platforms and institutions build inferred attributes about you from your digital behaviour — assumptions you never stated outright.

items.lead: Ask why, every time.
items.body: Develop the habit of questioning why you're shown a particular ad, recommendation, or treatment online — who is collecting the data behind it, and for what purpose.

items.lead: Audit what you share before you're asked to review it.
items.body: Regularly check the privacy settings on every account, app and service, share only what's strictly necessary, and be wary of requests for excessive permissions.

items.lead: Use tools that limit tracking, and clear what you no longer need.
items.body: Privacy-enhancing browsers, search engines and VPNs reduce what's collected in the first place; deleting old accounts and unused data removes what's already sitting there.

items.lead: Support the right to an explanation.
items.body: Back policies and regulation that give individuals the right to understand how an algorithmic decision affecting them was actually made.

items.lead: Push for systems that can be explained and audited.
items.body: Champion Explainable AI (XAI) research that makes models genuinely interpretable, and support independent audits of the algorithms used in high-stakes decisions — lending, hiring, criminal justice — to identify and mitigate bias.

items.lead: Know the regulations that already protect you.
items.body: Familiarise yourself with the data protection laws that give you specific rights over your own personal data.

items.lead: Challenge a decision, and back those who do it at scale.
items.body: If you believe an automated decision has treated you unfairly, seek information and challenge it through the channels available — and support the digital rights organisations working to protect those channels and promote ethical AI governance.

items.lead: Invest in what no platform mediates.
items.body: Deep, authentic relationships and activities that happen outside digital platforms are ground the algorithmic self can't reach.

items.lead: Anchor your worth in your own values, not the metrics.
items.body: Root your sense of self in your values, beliefs and experiences rather than external validation, and regularly reflect on how online narratives might be shaping your self-perception.

items.lead: Your algorithmic reputation is not who you are.
items.body: It's an inference, built from fragments — and it can be audited, challenged and outgrown, but only if you treat it as something to manage, not something to accept.

items.lead: Ask who created this and what they stand to gain.
items.body: Especially with content labelled 'native' or 'sponsored' — the format itself is built to blur the source.

items.lead: Look for the disclosure labels platforms are required to show.
items.body: 'Ad', 'sponsored', 'promoted' — small print doing a big job, easy to scroll straight past.

items.lead: Unfollow influencers whose content has turned commercial.
items.body: When a feed starts reading like a catalogue rather than a person, that shift is information.

items.lead: Install an ad blocker, even an imperfect one.
items.body: It won't catch everything, but it cuts the volume of intrusive advertising doing the shaping.

items.lead: Talk to people about the tactics you spot.
items.body: Collective awareness builds a resistance no single sceptical mind can manage alone.

items.lead: Studies what actually makes advertising and marketing effective.
items.body: The consumer-behaviour research behind why persuasion works on us.

items.lead: Builds the skills needed to critically read a media message.
items.body: The starting discipline for spotting manipulation before it lands.

items.lead: Examines the impact and ethics of influencer marketing.
items.body: Including how blurred the line to straightforward advertising has become.

items.lead: Tracks how digital tools and data shape political campaigns.
items.body: And the public opinion those campaigns are built to move.

items.lead: Uses big data and algorithms to study collective behaviour.
items.body: The same methods increasingly used to predict — and pre-empt — how a crowd will react.

items.lead: Become a cognitive sentinel, not a vulnerable target.
items.body: Healthy scepticism and a habit of questioning narratives protect more than your own judgement — a mind that isn't easily captured strengthens the collective one too.

items.lead: Recognise the manipulation before you react to it.
items.body: Modern attacks rarely start with code — they start with a fabricated scenario built on urgency, fear or impersonation of authority: a bank, a tax office, your own CEO. When one arrives, pause, then verify the request through an independent channel — call the organisation back on a publicly listed number, or type its website address in yourself.

items.lead: Treat every public detail as intelligence for your attacker.
items.body: Review your privacy settings and limit what you share, especially the details behind secret questions — a mother's maiden name, a pet's name, a birth city. The less you expose, the smaller the target, and the harder it becomes to build a phishing message that feels personal.

items.lead: Trust nothing until it's proven safe.
items.body: Assume every link, attachment and unexpected request could be a trap. Hover over a link to check its true destination before clicking, and confirm any attachment with the sender through a separate, trusted channel — a text message or a fresh phone call. Caution isn't cynicism; it's how you stay ahead of someone counting on your instinct to react quickly.

items.lead: Resilience isn't achieved through fear — it's built through fluency.
items.body: The digital fortress isn't built once and forgotten; it's maintained daily, through awareness, curiosity and consistent care. Make a Zero Trust mindset an everyday habit, and you stop being the weakest link in the chain — you become the most fortified.

items.lead: Know exactly where AI actually excels.
items.body: Pattern recognition, processing vast datasets, repetitive tasks, complex calculation and generating creative variations — text, images, code — are its real strengths; know them precisely rather than vaguely.

items.lead: Name what AI genuinely can't do.
items.body: It lacks true consciousness, emotional intelligence, nuanced context, genuine creativity beyond recombination, ethical reasoning, and the ability to operate reliably outside its training data without human guidance.

items.lead: Frame it as augmentation, not replacement.
items.body: Treat AI as a tool that enhances human performance and frees time for higher-level thinking — not a direct substitute for the judgement a role actually requires.

items.lead: Start small, with well-defined tasks.
items.body: Bring AI in for specific jobs first — drafting, data analysis, scheduling — and choose the tool that actually fits the task, weighing usability and integration, not just capability.

items.lead: Keep a human in the loop for anything that matters.
items.body: Treat AI suggestions as powerful input, not an absolute directive — critical decisions, ethical review and quality control still need a person with the authority to say no.

items.lead: Learn to prompt with precision.
items.body: The quality of what AI produces depends heavily on the quality of what you ask it — treat prompt engineering as a genuine skill, not an afterthought.

items.lead: Stay a continuous learner as the tools keep changing.
items.body: Build real AI literacy — how algorithms work at a working level, and what their ethical implications actually are — rather than treating today's version as the finished article.

items.lead: Sharpen the skills machines can't do.
items.body: As AI absorbs more routine work, prioritise critical thinking, creativity, complex communication, emotional intelligence and interdisciplinary collaboration — the capabilities that become more valuable, not less.

items.lead: Treat feedback as training, not just correction.
items.body: Give AI tools clear, constructive feedback to refine their output for your specific context — a diligent, literal assistant improves with direction, not silence.

items.lead: Mind what you actually feed into the system.
items.body: Be deliberate about data privacy and security, especially with cloud-based tools — know how your input is used and stored before you share it.

items.lead: Assume bias is present until you've checked.
items.body: AI models inherit and can amplify the biases in their training data — critically evaluate outputs for fairness and accuracy, especially in sensitive contexts.

items.lead: Say plainly when AI did the work.
items.body: Be transparent about AI's role in anything that might be read as human-made, and stay alert to the wider societal impact of adopting it — in your field and beyond.

items.lead: Notice when you're most focused during the day, and protect that window for your hardest work.
items.body: Schedule demanding tasks for the hours your mind is naturally sharpest, not whenever they happen to land on the calendar.

items.lead: Build a dedicated space for deep work, free of notifications and background noise.
items.body: A focus zone you enter deliberately, not one you hope to find amid the usual pings and digital temptations.

items.lead: Choose one task and stay with it, even for short stretches.
items.body: Every switch between tasks carries a hidden cost — single-tasking rebuilds the muscle that constant switching wears down.

items.lead: Treat sleep as a non-negotiable part of your routine, not the first thing you cut.
items.body: Adequate sleep is a critical input to focus and mental clarity — not a reward for finishing everything else.

items.lead: Break complex information into smaller pieces before you try to hold it all in mind.
items.body: Short-term memory has a real limit — respecting it prevents the overload that stalls thinking altogether.

items.lead: Studies selective, sustained and divided attention.
items.body: Including phenomena like inattentional blindness and change blindness.

items.lead: Researches the brain regions and neural networks behind attention.
items.body: Covering how focus is directed, maintained and shifted.

items.lead: Studies the limits of short-term memory, such as Miller's "Magic Number".
items.body: And what those limits mean for how information actually gets processed.

items.lead: Examines how sleep deprivation and sleep quality affect the mind.
items.body: Attention, memory, decision-making and overall cognitive performance are all at stake.

items.lead: Looks at whether mindfulness and meditation actually improve focus.
items.body: Alongside other cognitive training techniques aimed at reducing distractibility.

items.lead: This isn't about achieving perfect focus overnight.
items.body: It's about shifting from passive reaction to active observation. Your chaotic attention isn't a personal failing — it's a predictable consequence of your brain and the modern world. Building awareness reclaims agency and lays the groundwork for a more intentional life.

items.card: Assert Ownership of Your Digital Self
items.lead: Know what data is being collected about you.
items.body: Browsing history, location, purchases and biometric data all count.

items.card: Assert Ownership of Your Digital Self
items.lead: Scan privacy policies for the clauses that matter,
items.body: not the whole document — look for “third-party sharing” and “monetisation.”

items.card: Assert Ownership of Your Digital Self
items.lead: Learn the data rights that apply in your region.
items.body: You can request access, correction or deletion of your information.

items.card: Assert Ownership of Your Digital Self
items.lead: Use privacy settings and do-not-track features.
items.body: They limit collection and targeted advertising, even if imperfectly.

items.card: Assert Ownership of Your Digital Self
items.lead: Treat your face and voice as reproducible material.
items.body: Be cautious about sharing highly personal media publicly.

items.card: Assert Ownership of Your Digital Self
items.lead: Read the terms before any AI tool touches your image or voice.
items.body: Some platforms claim broad licences over what you upload.

items.card: Assert Ownership of Your Digital Self
items.lead: Think twice before handing over fingerprints or facial scans.
items.body: Know how that data is stored, and what misuse looks like.

items.card: Assert Ownership of Your Digital Self
items.lead: Watermark or sign your original work.
items.body: It gives you a way to track its use and establish ownership later.

items.card: Assert Ownership of Your Digital Self
items.lead: Be deliberate about what you post.
items.body: Everything you share becomes part of a permanent record — assume it can be archived, screenshotted or redistributed beyond your control.

items.card: Assert Ownership of Your Digital Self
items.lead: Keep professional and personal presences distinct.
items.body: Separate accounts and separate audiences give you separate control over how each version of you gets read.

items.card: Assert Ownership of Your Digital Self
items.lead: Search your own name and handles periodically.
items.body: See what's publicly visible, then request removal of anything outdated, inaccurate or never authorised.

items.card: Assert Ownership of Your Digital Self
items.lead: Revoke access you no longer remember granting.
items.body: Old app permissions and forgotten integrations to your accounts rarely get reviewed once granted.

items.card: Assert Ownership of Your Digital Self
items.lead: Keep up with what generative AI can now do.
items.body: The tools reshaping identity, privacy and synthetic media are moving faster than most people realise.

items.card: Assert Ownership of Your Digital Self
items.lead: Question content that feels too convenient.
items.body: Learn the visual and audio signs of a deepfake before you need to spot one under pressure.

items.card: Assert Ownership of Your Digital Self
items.lead: Share what you learn with people around you.
items.body: A more informed circle of friends and family is a genuinely harder target to exploit.

items.card: Assert Ownership of Your Digital Self
items.lead: Support policy that protects individual data rights.
items.body: Ethical AI development needs sustained public pressure, not just good intentions from inside the industry.

items.card: Practise the Three-Foot World in a Digital Age
items.lead: Notice what actually pulls your focus away from the present.
items.body: Turn off the notifications that don't earn their interruption, and make using technology something you choose deliberately rather than something you fall into.

items.card: Practise the Three-Foot World in a Digital Age
items.lead: Define the radius of action you can genuinely affect this week.
items.body: The tasks, conversations and relationships that sit within your sphere of influence — and, by naming them, the ones that sit outside it.

items.card: Practise the Three-Foot World in a Digital Age
items.lead: Put your time into the people you can actually reach.
items.body: Face-to-face, local and tangible interaction is where your presence changes something; be present where your presence matters.

items.card: Practise the Three-Foot World in a Digital Age
items.lead: When overwhelm hits, ask what you can touch, change or improve within the next three feet.
items.body: The question converts a general sense of helplessness into one specific action available to you today.

items.card: Practise the Three-Foot World in a Digital Age
items.lead: Write with a pen. Walk without headphones. Speak without a screen between you.
items.body: Cognitive depth rebuilds through sensory simplicity, not through a better-designed app.

items.card: Practise the Three-Foot World in a Digital Age
items.lead: Build services that keep a person within reach of the decision.
items.body: Physical presence, emotional proximity or localised decision-making each keep a service answerable to someone who can see its effect.

items.card: Practise the Three-Foot World in a Digital Age
items.lead: Push power and resources out to the frontline.
items.body: Schools, clinics, libraries and neighbourhood groups already know what their community needs; autonomy is what lets them act on it.

items.card: Practise the Three-Foot World in a Digital Age
items.lead: Simplify forms, processes and interfaces until anxiety stops being part of the transaction.
items.body: People should be able to understand and complete what you ask of them without needing help to do it.

items.card: Practise the Three-Foot World in a Digital Age
items.lead: Reward the initiatives that change something in the community this quarter.
items.body: Immediate local effect is a harder measure to report than an abstract KPI, and a more honest one.

items.card: Practise the Three-Foot World in a Digital Age
items.lead: Test policies and technologies in specific communities before you scale them.
items.body: The three-foot world is where real feedback lives; a pilot that never touches one tells you very little.

items.lead: Search each privacy policy for two questions: what data do they collect, and how do they use it.
items.body: Skip the legal boilerplate around them — those two sections carry almost everything you actually need to know.

items.lead: Use the data access and deletion rights a service actually offers you.
items.body: A right sitting unused in a settings menu protects nobody — request your data, or ask for it to be deleted.

items.lead: Try a browser or extension built to limit what gets tracked about you.
items.body: Small switches, a different browser, a tracker blocker, change how much of your activity gets collected by default.

items.lead: Support the companies that make their privacy controls clear and easy to use.
items.body: Where you spend your attention and your custom is itself a signal platforms read and respond to.

items.lead: Read consent requests instead of clicking straight through them.
items.body: Choose the granular option where one exists, rather than accepting the broadest default.

items.lead: Studies how data protection regulations get written, applied and enforced.
items.body: GDPR and CCPA are the most cited examples, but the same questions recur wherever the law tries to catch up.

items.lead: Develops cryptographic techniques and tools that limit what data has to be exposed.
items.body: The aim is data that stays useful without staying visible to everyone who touches it.

items.lead: Debates who actually owns your data, and what companies owe you because of it.
items.body: Legal and philosophical arguments about ownership, identity and the responsibilities of holding someone else's information.

items.lead: Traces how breaches happen once data has been aggregated at scale.
items.body: The bigger the collection, the bigger the target, and the more people affected when it fails.

items.lead: Studies how people's attitudes to privacy actually shape their digital habits.
items.body: The gap between what people say they want and what they click through is itself the subject.

items.lead: This isn't about reading every privacy policy end to end.
items.body: It's about becoming a digital citizen rather than a passive user — someone whose small, deliberate choices, and voice in the wider conversation, count as a vote for a digital world where technology serves people instead of exploiting them.

items.lead: Make it clear when someone is speaking to AI, not a person.
items.body: Build standards around transparency, inclusivity and consent, and give every user an easy way to escalate to a human.

items.lead: Bring community stakeholders into the room before the script is written.
items.body: Involve them in shaping a digital human's language, expressions and emotional responses, so bias in culture, race or gender doesn't get built in unnoticed.

items.lead: Test the language model and its affective computing regularly.
items.body: Look for unintended persuasion, exclusion or emotional profiling before the public finds it for you.

items.lead: Never trap a user inside a conversation with a machine.
items.body: Keep a visible, accessible route to a human on hand, especially once a case turns sensitive or complex.

items.lead: Track sentiment and stress signals through every interaction.
items.body: A digital human should ease the public's mental load, not quietly add to it.

items.lead: Insist on being told when you're talking to a non-human agent.
items.body: And demand the option to speak with a person when you need to.

items.lead: Call out a digital human when it gets something wrong.
items.body: Failing to understand you, excluding your dialect, or handling distress without any care are all worth reporting, not just tolerating.

items.lead: Push for transparency in who actually built and runs it.
items.body: Public, private or somewhere in between, accountability shouldn't be a mystery.

items.lead: Take part in the civic conversation about digital empathy in public services.
items.body: An interaction with the state should never be a black box.

items.lead: Ask where a piece of information actually came from before you believe it.
items.body: Be especially wary when it feels too perfect, too sensational, or oddly tailored to exactly what interests you.

items.lead: Check for any label or disclaimer that marks content as AI-generated or AI-assisted.
items.body: These disclosures are appearing more often — reading past them defeats the point of them existing.

items.lead: Cross-check anything that matters against more than one reputable source.
items.body: A claim that only appears in one place, however confidently stated, hasn't earned your trust yet.

items.lead: Learn to recognise the common forms AI-generated content takes.
items.body: Deepfakes and AI-written text each leave their own tells once you know what to look for.

items.lead: Talk to the people around you about what generative AI is doing to information and trust.
items.body: The conversation sharpens your own scepticism, and theirs.

items.lead: Studies the ethical questions generative AI raises, including bias, misinformation and accountability.
items.body: The questions recur wherever a system now makes a judgement call a person used to make instead.

items.lead: Studies how the brain processes and stores information.
items.body: And how AI-generated content might influence or manipulate that process without you noticing.

items.lead: Studies what happens to work and creativity when humans and AI create content together.
items.body: The interesting question is what each side actually contributes, not just that the two now work together.

items.lead: Traces how generative AI is used to create and spread false narratives.
items.body: And the strategies researchers and platforms are testing to combat them.

items.lead: Develops curricula and tools that help people understand and critically engage with AI technologies.
items.body: The aim is a public that can question a system's output, not just consume it.

items.lead: This isn't about achieving perfect objectivity.
items.body: It's about becoming an active sense-maker rather than a passive consumer of whatever the feed curates — building your own understanding through critical thinking, varied sources and conscious choice, so your beliefs stay yours rather than an algorithm's design.

items.lead: Isolate your smart devices on their own network.
items.body: Create a separate, dedicated guest Wi-Fi network for every IoT device — cameras, thermostats, speakers — so a compromised device can't move laterally into your laptop, your work systems or your financial data.

items.lead: Replace every factory password before you switch a device on.
items.body: Default logins like “admin” or “123456” are the first thing an attacker tries — give every device its own strong, unique credential the moment you set it up.

items.lead: Buy from vendors who keep patching.
items.body: Prioritise companies with a proven record of security updates and transparent privacy policies, and know when a device's end-of-life arrives — the point its manufacturer stops issuing patches — so you can retire it before it becomes a liability.

items.lead: Every device you add to your network is a door — the fewer left unlocked, the smaller the target.
items.body: Segmentation, unique credentials and knowing a device's end-of-life aren't extra precautions — they're what keeps the smart home's convenience from becoming its liability.

items.lead: Notice how each platform makes you feel, not just what it shows you.
items.body: Pay attention to the interactions that shift your mood or self-perception, and name the content or exchanges that reliably trigger inadequacy or pressure to conform.

items.lead: Check your online persona against who you actually are.
items.body: Regularly ask whether your digital presence still lines up with your core values and the person you're trying to be offline.

items.lead: Decide what you share before a platform decides it for you.
items.body: Curate with purpose rather than letting a feed's defaults set your online identity, and segment which facets of yourself belong on which network.

items.lead: Take real breaks from your digital self.
items.body: Schedule regular disconnection so your offline self, your physical surroundings and your real-world relationships get their own uninterrupted time.

items.lead: Name your values before a platform names them for you.
items.body: Articulate what actually gives your life meaning, independent of likes, followers or any other digital metric.

items.lead: Spend real time on things a screen can't measure.
items.body: Invest deliberately in offline hobbies and relationships that build genuine connection and a sense of accomplishment no algorithm can touch.

items.lead: Set limits before the platform sets them for you.
items.body: Establish clear boundaries on screen time and engagement, and be ruthless about unfollowing or muting anything that damages your self-esteem.

items.lead: Treat your privacy settings as an active decision, not a default.
items.body: Understand what each platform actually shares, and stay alert to what oversharing costs your personal and professional identity later.

items.lead: Invest first in the people in the room.
items.body: Prioritise face-to-face conversation and shared experience with family and friends over anything a screen can offer instead.

items.lead: Let technology open real relationships, not replace them.
items.body: Use online tools to bridge toward offline connection, and turn genuine online acquaintances into people you actually meet.

items.lead: Notice what actually sends you reaching for your phone.
items.body: Boredom, a notification, a moment of stress — name the trigger and you can start to interrupt it, rather than acting on it automatically.

items.lead: Name the reward you're actually chasing — a like, new content, a message.
items.body: Ask honestly whether it lines up with what you want from your time, or just with what keeps you opening the app.

items.lead: Put a small obstacle between yourself and the compulsive reach.
items.body: Remove the app from your home screen, log out after each use, turn off the notification — friction a habit has to work around.

items.lead: Swap the digital habit for an offline one the moment the urge arrives.
items.body: Choose something that actually serves you, not just whatever isn't a screen.

items.lead: Tell the people close to you what you've learned about the Hook Model and addictive design.
items.body: Shared awareness makes healthier habits easier to keep, for you and for them.

items.lead: Studies how cues, routines and rewards drive human behaviour.
items.body: Particularly revealing once you apply it to a habit that plays out entirely on a screen.

items.lead: Studies how design choices are used deliberately to shape what you do next.
items.body: The interface in front of you was built by someone whose job was influencing your behaviour, not just making the product usable.

items.lead: Studies the clinical and psychological impact of problematic internet and phone use.
items.body: Where habit tips into compulsion, and what the evidence says actually helps.

items.lead: Studies how game mechanics get applied outside games to drive engagement.
items.body: Points, streaks and levels didn't arrive in your apps by accident — they arrived because they work.

items.lead: Studies the brain's dopamine pathways and their role in seeking behaviour.
items.body: The chemistry behind the reach explains why willpower alone rarely beats a well-designed reward loop.

items.lead: This isn't about achieving flawless scepticism.
items.body: It's about becoming an active filter rather than a passive receiver — someone who chooses deliberately what to accept, question and discard, so what shapes your view of the world is actually yours.

items.card: Navigate the Geopolitics of Technology and Global Governance
items.lead: Build dedicated channels for technology diplomacy.
items.body: Formal and informal forums that bring governments, companies, civil society and academia together work through a technology's impact before deployment, not after.

items.card: Navigate the Geopolitics of Technology and Global Governance
items.lead: Find shared definitions before you need them.
items.body: Common understandings of ethical AI, data governance and cybersecurity norms across different political and cultural contexts make later disagreement something you can actually resolve.

items.card: Navigate the Geopolitics of Technology and Global Governance
items.lead: Resist the fragmentation of the internet.
items.body: Open, interoperable standards keep systems connected across borders; a balkanised internet just hands each fragment to whoever controls it.

items.card: Navigate the Geopolitics of Technology and Global Governance
items.lead: Diversify the supply chains that hold everything up.
items.body: Work multilaterally to reduce single points of failure in critical technology supply chains, without retreating into protectionism to do it.

items.card: Navigate the Geopolitics of Technology and Global Governance
items.lead: Design regulation that can move as fast as the technology.
items.body: Iterative, flexible agreements outlast rules written for a specific technology that will be obsolete before they're ratified.

items.card: Navigate the Geopolitics of Technology and Global Governance
items.lead: Regulate outcomes, not technologies.
items.body: A focus on impact rather than mechanism gives bodies like the UN, ITU and WTO the mandate to keep pace as new technologies arrive, rather than rewriting the rulebook each time.

items.card: Navigate the Geopolitics of Technology and Global Governance
items.lead: Hold human rights standards above sovereignty claims.
items.body: Privacy, freedom of expression and non-discrimination shouldn't bend to whichever jurisdiction happens to be enforcing them.

items.card: Navigate the Geopolitics of Technology and Global Governance
items.lead: Push for ethical AI treaties with actual teeth.
items.body: International agreements on autonomous weapons, surveillance and algorithmic bias matter more, not less, once the technological capacity to act on them is already there.

items.card: Navigate the Geopolitics of Technology and Global Governance
items.lead: The rules for this technology are being written right now, by whoever shows up.
items.body: Waiting for governance to catch up isn't neutral — it's a decision to let someone else's interests fill the gap.

items.lead: Set clear times for disconnecting from work email and social media.
items.body: Use 'do not disturb' modes to make the boundary automatic rather than something you have to enforce by willpower alone.

items.lead: Schedule dedicated blocks of uninterrupted time for complex tasks.
items.body: Free the block from digital distractions entirely — deep work and partial attention can't coexist in the same window.

items.lead: Take short breaks or longer periods away from screens on a regular basis.
items.body: The reset isn't about willpower during the break — it's about what resuming with a clearer mind lets you notice afterwards.

items.lead: Engage in activities that don't involve a screen at all.
items.body: A different kind of engagement — one that doesn't compete for the same attention a feed is built to hold.

items.lead: Pay attention to how different digital interactions actually make you feel.
items.body: If a platform consistently leaves you anxious or inadequate, that's information worth acting on, not ignoring.

items.lead: Build a consistent bedtime routine, screens off for at least an hour before sleep.
items.body: The last hour of the day is also the hour most vulnerable to a feed with nothing better to do than hold you there.

items.lead: Studies the links between technology use and conditions like anxiety, depression and loneliness.
items.body: The correlations are well documented; the harder question is which uses cause harm and which merely track it.

items.lead: Studies how information overload and multitasking affect cognitive performance and decision-making.
items.body: Every open tab and notification is a small tax on the working memory you need for the task in front of you.

items.lead: Researches the brain mechanisms behind sustained attention, distraction and mental exhaustion.
items.body: Attention is a finite resource with a biological cost — fatigue isn't a character flaw, it's a measurable limit.

items.lead: Studies which strategies for reducing screen time actually work, and which only feel like they do.
items.body: The evidence base for most popular interventions is thinner than the wellness industry suggests.

items.lead: Studies how technology and the attention economy are reshaping work patterns and personal boundaries.
items.body: The boundary between work and rest didn't erode by accident — the always-on expectation was built into the tools.

items.lead: The goal isn't to reject the digital world you live in.
items.body: It's to move from captive participant to intentional steward of your own mind and time — building a life shaped by your values rather than whatever's engineered to hold your attention next.

items.lead: Learn to spot the design patterns built to hook you.
items.body: Infinite scroll, streaks, notifications and fear of missing out are engineered, not accidental — name them when you see them.

items.lead: Audit where your attention actually goes.
items.body: Use screen time reports or your own journal to compare real usage against what you intended, and remember a 'free' product is usually paid for with your attention.

items.lead: Turn off what's designed to pull you back in.
items.body: Disable non-essential notifications, autoplay and personalised recommendations, and use ad blockers or focus tools to blunt algorithmic influence.

items.lead: Build routines for how and when you engage.
items.body: Curate your feeds ruthlessly, and design specific windows for checking platforms rather than letting them interrupt you at will.

items.lead: Protect blocks of time a notification can't reach.
items.body: Dedicate uninterrupted stretches to deep work, creative pursuits or offline conversation, and defend them from digital intrusion.

items.lead: Choose participation over consumption.
items.body: Favour creating, discussing and learning over passive scrolling, and seek out slower spaces that reward thoughtful discussion over rapid-fire engagement.

items.lead: Audit your own product for manipulation, not just usability.
items.body: Regularly assess features for manipulative patterns and their real impact on a user's mental health, time and agency.

items.lead: Measure value created, not just time spent.
items.body: Give users clear, robust controls over notifications, algorithms and usage limits, and shift your own metrics toward genuine value and wellbeing.

items.lead: Say plainly what data you collect and why it benefits the user.
items.body: Replace opaque terms and conditions with a clear value exchange, and experiment with business models that don't depend solely on advertising or extraction.

items.lead: Champion the user's right to their own data.
items.body: Support policies and technologies that give people real ownership and control over their personal data, including the right to decide how it's used.

items.lead: Teach users how the attention economy actually works.
items.body: Build features and prompts that grow digital literacy and critical thinking directly into the product, not as a separate education campaign.

items.lead: Lead internally the way you ask users to behave.
items.body: Make user wellbeing and ethical practice part of your own culture and product development, not just your public messaging.

items.lead: Audit what your apps and devices actually collect.
items.body: Review permissions regularly, and understand not just what data is gathered but how it gets used.

items.lead: Question every anticipatory suggestion an interface makes.
items.body: Ask whether it serves your interests, or is quietly shaping your behaviour toward someone else's.

items.lead: Choose deliberate interaction over default convenience.
items.body: Not every command needs to be anticipated — sometimes acting for yourself is the point.

items.lead: Demand plain explanations of how a system operates.
items.body: Opaque terms and conditions are not a substitute for genuine transparency.

items.lead: Use the granular controls a technology actually offers.
items.body: If it won't let you adjust anticipation or data collection, treat that as a reason to look elsewhere.

items.lead: Set times and zones where anticipatory interfaces switch off.
items.body: Protecting some cognitive autonomy means occasionally living without constant digital interpretation.

items.lead: Tell developers directly when a design feels intrusive.
items.body: Specific, constructive feedback shifts a product faster than silent frustration ever will.

items.lead: Back the products and organisations built around user control.
items.body: Support for privacy-respecting technology has to show up in what people actually choose to use.

items.lead: Talk to the people around you about what these systems do.
items.body: A wider public conversation moves the industry — individual vigilance alone doesn't.

items.lead: Map the emotional cost of anticipatory features, not just the journey.
items.body: Consider what each prediction does to a person's agency, privacy and wellbeing.

items.lead: Explain why the system is anticipating, and let people override it.
items.body: A prediction that hides its own reasoning invites suspicion, not trust.

items.lead: Make consent explicit before collecting anything significant.
items.body: Opt-in has to be the default, not a setting buried where nobody finds it.

items.lead: Audit algorithms for bias on a regular schedule.
items.body: Unintended discrimination compounds quietly if nobody is checking for it.

items.lead: Show your working on how decisions get made.
items.body: Users deserve some visibility into the logic behind what a system anticipates for them.

items.lead: Keep a human able to override the machine.
items.body: No automated system should become impossible to contest or correct.

items.lead: Collect only what the service genuinely needs.
items.body: State plainly what's gathered and why, rather than defaulting to maximum collection.

items.lead: Store data as securely as the highest standard demands.
items.body: Ethical retention isn't optional once a system starts holding people's information.

items.lead: Let people take their data with them, or delete it outright.
items.body: Portability and deletion on request are basic tests of who actually owns the information.

items.lead: Notice the psychological tactics at work in the ads you actually encounter.
items.body: Emotional appeals, scarcity, authority — the techniques repeat once you know to look for them, across TV, print and online.

items.lead: Pause before a purchase and ask whether you need it, or whether the desire was manufactured.
items.body: Marketing's job is to make a want feel like a need — the pause is what tells the two apart.

items.lead: Look into how major brands built their identity and captured loyalty over time.
items.body: The playbook is decades old; seeing its origins makes today's version easier to recognise.

items.lead: Talk to older generations about how advertising has changed over their lifetime.
items.body: Their memory of what persuasion used to look like is a useful baseline for measuring what it's become.

items.lead: Watch for when an idea is being engineered into public discourse rather than arrived at.
items.body: Public relations works best when it's invisible — spotting the campaign is the first step to weighing it fairly.

items.lead: Studies how advertising techniques and agencies developed, and their impact on consumer culture.
items.body: The industry that shapes today's attention economy has a documented history — none of this started with the internet.

items.lead: Researches the origins of PR, including figures like Edward Bernays and their influence on public opinion.
items.body: Modern persuasion techniques were formalised nearly a century ago, often explicitly modelled on propaganda.

items.lead: Studies early experiments and theories on consumer behaviour, motivation and decision-making.
items.body: Much of what platforms use today was tested on shoppers long before it was tested on scrollers.

items.lead: Traces the historical development of branding strategies and their role in market competition.
items.body: A brand is a persuasion structure built to outlast any single campaign — understanding it changes how loyalty reads.

items.lead: Studies how industrialisation and mass production gave rise to consumer societies.
items.body: Attention became a commodity long before data did — the commodification of information and attention is the same story continued.

items.lead: Your attention has always been a resource with a cost.
items.body: Recognising the exchange — rather than accepting it as invisible — is what moves you from product to a discerning participant in it.

items.lead: Train for the scenario, not the slogan.
items.body: Move beyond generic awareness videos — regular, scenario-based sessions teach employees to spot mismatched URLs, false urgency and unusual tone before they click.

items.lead: Treat failure as a teaching moment.
items.body: Run routine phishing simulations and use the outcomes to educate, not discipline — punishing a click teaches people to hide it, not to avoid it next time.

items.lead: Build a blame-free reporting culture.
items.body: Make 'see something, say something' real: every suspicious link reported early is a breach prevented, and speaking up should never carry a cost.

items.lead: Build the response team before the breach.
items.body: IT, legal, communications, operations and HR each have a role in a crisis — nobody should be learning theirs when the alarm sounds.

items.lead: Decide who speaks, before anyone needs to.
items.body: Prepare transparent, pre-approved statements for employees, customers, regulators and media so a crisis doesn't also become a communications failure.

items.lead: Rehearse the whole lifecycle.
items.body: Detection, containment, eradication, recovery and post-incident review — test the plan with tabletop exercises and live simulations, because an untested plan is an unproven one.

items.lead: Verify before you onboard.
items.body: Require documentation of a vendor's security maturity — certifications, policies and incident response protocols — before granting them access to your systems.

items.lead: Make resilience a contractual obligation.
items.body: Specify encryption, breach notification and continuous vulnerability assessment in every vendor contract; don't leave security as an assumption.

items.lead: Grant access on need, not convenience.
items.body: Review vendor permissions regularly and revoke credentials the moment they're no longer required — a forgotten login is an open door.

items.lead: Resilience isn't a compliance checkbox — it's a competitive advantage.
items.body: The most secure enterprises don't chase every new threat; they build adaptable systems, nurture vigilance, and plan for recovery before the crisis hits. Security signals governance maturity, and in markets where trust determines longevity, that maturity is the differentiator.

items.card: Engage with Human Augmentation for Cognitive Enhancement
items.lead: Name the specific thing you're trying to improve.
items.body: Memory, focus, learning speed, sensory perception — a vague ambition to be "more enhanced" leads to tools adopted for their own sake, not for what they're actually for.

items.card: Engage with Human Augmentation for Cognitive Enhancement
items.lead: Weigh the ethics before you weigh the benefit.
items.body: Ask whether the augmentation is safe and equitable, and whether it aligns with your own values, before asking whether it works.

items.card: Engage with Human Augmentation for Cognitive Enhancement
items.lead: Separate the evidenced from the speculative.
items.body: Smart wearables, brain-computer interfaces, nootropics and AI-driven learning tools sit at very different points on the evidence spectrum — know which one you're actually being offered.

items.card: Engage with Human Augmentation for Cognitive Enhancement
items.lead: Check what it does with your cognitive data before you check what it does for you.
items.body: A tool that reads focus, memory or attention is also collecting some of the most personal data there is. Prioritise the ones with real privacy protection built in.

items.card: Engage with Human Augmentation for Cognitive Enhancement
items.lead: Start with the lowest-impact option available.
items.body: Smart notepads and focus apps before brain-computer interfaces. Augmentation is a skill to be learned, not a switch to be flipped.

items.card: Engage with Human Augmentation for Cognitive Enhancement
items.lead: Keep the fundamentals in place underneath it.
items.body: Sleep, nutrition, exercise and stress management don't get replaced by a tool that complements them — monitor whether the augmentation is actually adding to those foundations or quietly eroding them.

items.card: Engage with Human Augmentation for Cognitive Enhancement
items.lead: Keep your unaugmented thinking in working order.
items.body: Over-reliance risks diminishing the very capacity the tool was meant to support — notice if you're becoming more efficient at tasks while becoming less capable without the tool.

items.card: Engage with Human Augmentation for Cognitive Enhancement
items.lead: Advocate for access, not just adoption.
items.body: Beneficial augmentation technologies won't reach everyone by default. Push for policies that make fair access to them part of the plan, not an afterthought.

items.card: Engage with Human Augmentation for Cognitive Enhancement
items.lead: Augmentation amplifies whatever intention you bring to it.
items.body: Clarity about what you're enhancing, and why, is the difference between a tool that deepens your judgement and one that quietly replaces it.

items.lead: Review your online accounts and delete the ones you no longer use.
items.body: For everything that stays active, strengthen the password and turn on multi-factor authentication — an old account nobody remembers is still a door nobody's watching.

items.lead: Turn on two-factor authentication for email, banking and social media.
items.body: These are the accounts that unlock everything else — a second factor here is the strongest single lock available to you.

items.lead: Find out how your biometric data is actually stored before you hand over a fingerprint or a face scan.
items.body: Unlike a password, a compromised fingerprint can't be reset — know what you're trusting a device or service to protect.

items.lead: Try a VPN, a privacy-focused browser or a secure messaging app for a week.
items.body: See what the difference actually feels like before deciding whether it's worth keeping.

items.lead: Decide what should happen to your accounts and data after you're gone.
items.body: Most platforms have a legacy or memorialisation setting — the choice sits with you until you make it, then it defaults to whatever the platform decides.

items.lead: Studies new authentication methods and the defences against identity theft and account takeover.
items.body: The tools protecting your accounts are changing faster than most people update their passwords.

items.lead: Studies how privacy gets built into a system from the start, rather than added afterwards.
items.body: Privacy by design shapes what a product can do with your data before you ever click accept.

items.lead: Explores blockchain-based and other decentralised approaches to managing identity.
items.body: The aim is an identity you hold and control directly, rather than one issued and verified by a single company.

items.lead: Studies how to design security that people will actually use correctly.
items.body: The strongest protection in theory is worth little if it's too awkward for anyone to keep using it.

items.lead: Investigates how digital identity crimes happen and how they get prevented.
items.body: Understanding how identity theft is actually carried out is the fastest way to see where your own exposure sits.

items.lead: This isn't about performing a perfect persona.
items.body: It's about becoming the conscious author of your own identity — closing the distance between who you are and who you present yourself to be, so your digital identity reflects you rather than an algorithm's incentives.

items.card: Defend Your Identity from Theft and Impersonation
items.lead: Move past passwords and static biometrics alone.
items.body: Build multi-modal, context-aware identity systems that weigh behavioural cues and provenance chains, not just a single credential.

items.card: Defend Your Identity from Theft and Impersonation
items.lead: Put a legal penalty on malicious digital cloning.
items.body: Create legislation that defines and penalises the deliberate creation or use of deepfakes, voice simulations and digital clones.

items.card: Defend Your Identity from Theft and Impersonation
items.lead: Make synthetic media identifiable by default.
items.body: Encourage watermarking of AI-generated content and maintain public registries of official synthetic personas.

items.card: Defend Your Identity from Theft and Impersonation
items.lead: Give investigators more than forensic computing skills.
items.body: Blend forensic computing with psychological analysis, narrative detection and deep learning literacy.

items.card: Defend Your Identity from Theft and Impersonation
items.lead: Never let identity determinations run fully automated.
items.body: Ensure human oversight in systems making high-stakes identity decisions, especially in immigration, welfare or justice.

items.card: Defend Your Identity from Theft and Impersonation
items.lead: Be cautious with your biometric, visual and voice data.
items.body: Once uploaded, any of it can be replicated — think before you share your face, your voice or your fingerprints online.

items.card: Defend Your Identity from Theft and Impersonation
items.lead: Treat convincing content with a healthy question first.
items.body: Ask whether what you're seeing could be synthetic, and use tools or plug-ins built to verify authenticity.

items.card: Defend Your Identity from Theft and Impersonation
items.lead: Advocate for legal ownership over your own digital likeness.
items.body: Push for laws that treat it as your intellectual property, giving you the right to license or block its use.

items.card: Defend Your Identity from Theft and Impersonation
items.lead: Choose products that are honest about synthetic media.
items.body: Promote platforms that disclose their use of synthetic media and uphold anti-impersonation safeguards.

items.card: Defend Your Identity from Theft and Impersonation
items.lead: Equip the people around you to recognise manipulated content.
items.body: Focus especially on the very young and the elderly, and support reporting manipulated content when you see it.

items.lead: Communicate clearly how systems work.
items.body: Explain what data they collect, how it's used, and who benefits — without jargon or legalese.

items.lead: Prioritise explainable AI over black boxes.
items.body: Choose systems that can explain their decisions and outputs in terms a person can actually follow.

items.lead: Adopt open standards and protocols.
items.body: Open-source software, open APIs and standardised formats allow real scrutiny and interoperability across systems.

items.lead: Log every critical operation and data flow.
items.body: Immutable audit trails let the record be checked and verified after the fact, not just trusted in the moment.

items.lead: Collect only the data a system actually needs.
items.body: Delete it once it's no longer necessary for the system's stated purpose.

items.lead: Give users granular control over their own data.
items.body: Let people choose, specifically and knowingly, what's shared and with whom.

items.lead: Design for understanding, not just use.
items.body: Interfaces should let people challenge and manage their interactions with a system, not just operate inside it.

items.lead: Build privacy into the architecture from day one.
items.body: It has to be structural, not a policy bolted on after the system already exists.

items.lead: Bring in independent third-party audits.
items.body: For critical systems, make external review of algorithms, data governance and security mandatory, not optional.

items.lead: Pay people to find what you missed.
items.body: Bug bounties and responsible disclosure programmes turn outside scrutiny into an asset, not a threat.

items.lead: Measure fairness against a shared benchmark.
items.body: Industry-wide metrics let a system's ethical performance be compared, not just asserted.

items.lead: Name who owns each system, end to end.
items.body: Design, deployment and ongoing operation each need a clear owner — a blame vacuum helps no one.

items.lead: Assess the impact before and during deployment.
items.body: Regular algorithmic impact assessments should weigh the societal, ethical and human rights consequences, not just the technical ones.

items.lead: Back independent bodies with real power to intervene.
items.body: Regulators, ombudsmen and oversight committees only help if they can act on systemic failure, not just observe it.

items.lead: Give people a real route to redress.
items.body: Anyone affected by an automated decision needs a clear, accessible way to complain, appeal and be heard.

items.lead: Teach ethics alongside engineering, not after it.
items.body: Training should weigh societal impact as seriously as technical capability, in design and management too.

items.lead: Stand up an internal ethics review board.
items.body: A red team that looks for harm before launch is worth more than one that explains it afterwards.

items.lead: Protect the people who raise concerns.
items.body: Strong whistleblower protections make it safe to flag unethical or harmful practice before it ships.

items.lead: Reward trustworthy design, not just fast design.
items.body: Grants, certifications and procurement preferences can make responsible technology the commercially smart choice too.

items.card: Co-create Experiences of Efficiency and Equity
items.lead: Pay conscious attention to every service interaction.
items.body: Note the pain points, the inefficiencies, and the moments that worked unexpectedly well.

items.card: Co-create Experiences of Efficiency and Equity
items.lead: Give feedback that names what happened, not just how you felt.
items.body: Say what worked or failed, why it mattered to you, and how it could change — through the formal channels, not just a complaint.

items.card: Co-create Experiences of Efficiency and Equity
items.lead: Name inequity when you see it, not just inconvenience.
items.body: If a service excludes, discriminates against, or simply fails certain groups, say so and back the case for inclusive design.

items.card: Co-create Experiences of Efficiency and Equity
items.lead: Volunteer for pilot programmes when you can.
items.body: Real-world feedback from an actual trial is worth more than a survey after the fact.

items.card: Co-create Experiences of Efficiency and Equity
items.lead: Join a user panel or focus group.
items.body: A seat in the room designing the service is worth more than a comment on the finished one.

items.card: Co-create Experiences of Efficiency and Equity
items.lead: Explain your own circumstances plainly.
items.body: Providers can only design for the range of users they actually understand.

items.card: Co-create Experiences of Efficiency and Equity
items.lead: Use the new digital channels, but keep judging them.
items.body: Chatbots, portals and virtual assistants earn trust through what they do, not what they promise.

items.card: Co-create Experiences of Efficiency and Equity
items.lead: Ask how your data is being used, every time.
items.body: Transparency and privacy aren't features to be grateful for — they're conditions to demand.

items.card: Co-create Experiences of Efficiency and Equity
items.lead: Back services that talk to each other, with your consent.
items.body: Interoperability between departments removes the redundancy of repeating yourself to each one.

items.card: Co-create Experiences of Efficiency and Equity
items.lead: Put human-centred design at the centre of the process.
items.body: Journey mapping, persona work and rapid prototyping belong at the start, not bolted on afterwards.

items.card: Co-create Experiences of Efficiency and Equity
items.lead: Reorganise around the user's journey, not your own departments.
items.body: Break down the silos that make seamless service delivery impossible internally.

items.card: Co-create Experiences of Efficiency and Equity
items.lead: Track experience and equity, not just throughput.
items.body: Satisfaction, ease of use and fair access matter alongside — not instead of — efficiency.

items.card: Co-create Experiences of Efficiency and Equity
items.lead: Use AI to anticipate need, not just respond to it.
items.body: Personalised, proactive support only earns trust with real transparency and user control over data.

items.card: Co-create Experiences of Efficiency and Equity
items.lead: Automate the low-value work to free up your people.
items.body: Automation should liberate staff for complex cases and empathy-driven work, not replace judgement.

items.card: Co-create Experiences of Efficiency and Equity
items.lead: Use AR and VR where guidance genuinely benefits from it.
items.body: Immersive training and step-by-step virtual repair guides help most in situations that are hardest to explain in text.

items.card: Co-create Experiences of Efficiency and Equity
items.lead: Let data expose inequity, not just optimise routing.
items.body: The same analytics that streamline delivery can and should surface where access and outcomes are already unequal.

items.card: Co-create Experiences of Efficiency and Equity
items.lead: Give frontline staff the autonomy to actually solve problems.
items.body: Tools and training mean little without the authority to use them on a complex case.

items.card: Co-create Experiences of Efficiency and Equity
items.lead: Build feedback loops that actually change the service.
items.body: A learning organisation lets user interactions and operational data inform real redesign and policy, not just a report.

items.card: Co-create Experiences of Efficiency and Equity
items.lead: Be plain about standards, timelines and how decisions get made.
items.body: Clear channels for redress and public accountability are what make transparency more than a word.

items.lead: Review your app permissions regularly.
items.body: Check and adjust what each app can access — especially location and notifications.

items.lead: Create friction before you open distracting apps.
items.body: Move them off your home screen, or bury them in a folder that costs an extra tap.

items.lead: Use the well-being tools already built into your phone.
items.body: Screen time trackers and app limits turn invisible habits into something you can see and set boundaries around.

items.lead: Set fixed phone-free times or zones.
items.body: The dinner table, the bedroom — anywhere the phone is put away on principle, not just when you remember.

items.lead: Question every recommendation before you follow it.
items.body: Pause and ask whether it matches your real interests, or whether it's just built to keep you scrolling.

items.lead: Research on user experience design specific to mobile devices.
items.body: Covers notification design, app usability and touch interfaces.

items.lead: Studies on how computing is woven into everyday environments.
items.body: Wearable tech and the Internet of Things, and their impact on attention.

items.lead: Examines the privacy implications of services that track your location.
items.body: The behavioural impact of apps built on real-time geographical data.

items.lead: Studies the effectiveness and biases of AI-driven recommendations.
items.body: The ethical questions behind what content and products get suggested to you.

items.lead: Research into the mechanisms and prevalence of compulsive smartphone use.
items.body: And its effects on mental health.

items.lead: The aim isn’t to abandon your phone — it’s to become the architect of your own attention.
items.body: Once its influence is visible, you can trade passive reaction for active choice, and dependency for intentionality.

items.lead: Name the values a system must uphold before you build it.
items.body: Articulate the human values it should serve — fairness, privacy, safety, respect, autonomy — and the harms it must avoid, before development starts.

items.lead: Bring diverse stakeholders into the design process itself.
items.body: Ethicists, social scientists, affected communities and users all shape what “ethical requirements” actually means — not just the engineering team.

items.lead: Translate abstract principles into measurable specifications.
items.body: Work collaboratively to turn ethical principles into concrete technical constraints an engineer can actually build to.

items.lead: Collect training data ethically, with explicit consent.
items.body: Avoid discriminatory or biased sources from the outset — cleaning up biased data afterwards is harder than not collecting it.

items.lead: Audit datasets for bias before they train the system.
items.body: Correct what you find through re-sampling, auditing or synthetic data generation, not after deployment reveals the problem.

items.lead: Build privacy by design into the data pipeline.
